Read 2026-11-18 from all 274 kept chats in `gs://prod-jusprin-v2` (all from 2.0.0). 17 chats from 12 people asked the AI for another language (Portuguese 15, French 2).

- 15 asked the AI to *answer* in their language. It switched at once every time; the project prompt says "Reply in the person's language" (`AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`).
- 2 (users 264295, 264614) asked for the app's *screens* in Portuguese. The AI read the `guide-the-app` skill and gave Preferences › Appearance › Language › Português (Brasil) › Restart now, matching `docs/guide/the-app.md`. But both already had `uiLanguage` pt_BR (the app_config `language` value, sent only in file-load reports).
- 11 of the 12 people already had the app set to their language. Cause of the English screens: 2.0.0 shipped without JusPrin's own catalogs (`Localization/native/pt_BR.po`, `pages/pt_BR.po` added in 00953649de, which is in 2.0.1).
- 6 chats got an English first reply to a bare printer name although the app was pt_BR. `printerInstructions.ts` has no reply-language rule and ordinary turns carry no app language. Not reproduced.

**Why:** Kenneth asked for a tool to change app settings (language) and then said: if the AI answers well from the docs, no tool is needed.
**How to apply:** no app-settings tool was built; the evidence says one would not have helped. Script: scratchpad `lang.py` pattern (grep person messages for language words). Related: [[app-guide-for-ai-and-people]], [[jusprin-chat-capture-design]].

name: history-trimming-by-size
description: 2026-10-15 5cf784d30b on local jusprin-newui (unpushed) - chat history to the model trimmed by a 64 KiB budget in three stages; kHistoryMessages (20 entries) is gone.
metadata:
  node_type: memory

  originSessionId: 8ff9449f-9ac5-4ce1-aa3b-d8b1da0ac594
  modified: 2026-10-16T03:15:22.605Z
---

`AgentHost::make_agent_request` no longer keeps "the last 20 entries". The history has a 64 KiB budget, measured as the serialized entries, and is trimmed only when over it. Three stages, each stopping once the history fits: results of calls older than the last two assistant turns become the "not repeated here; call the tool again" note, oldest first; then whole calls are dropped, oldest first; then the oldest words, never the newest message. A turn means the assistant messages that share one `in_reply_to`.

The budget comes from 12 live 3-turn chats (model-nature-probe transcripts), which replayed at 9 to 33 KB with no result over 10 KB. Tests are in tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp, tagged `[history]`. The untracked report is report-history-trimming.md in worktree nice-morse-0dfae8.

**Why:** the old cut dropped the person's words while 16 KiB tool payloads stayed, and could send about 320 KiB.
**How to apply:** older memories that mention the 20-entry cap, such as [[printer-chat-tool-history-replay]], are stale on that point. Whether the model actually calls a tool again when it sees the note has not been measured live.

But both already had `uiLanguage` pt_BR (the app_config `language` value, sent only in file-load reports).
- 11 of the 12 people already had the app set to their language. Cause of the English screens: 2.0.0 shipped without JusPrin's own catalogs (`Localization/native/pt_BR.po`, `pages/pt_BR.po` added in 00953649de, which is in 2.0.1).
- 6 chats got an English first reply to a bare printer name although the app was pt_BR. `printerInstructions.ts` has no reply-language rule and ordinary turns carry no app language. Not reproduced.

**Why:** Kenneth asked for a tool to change app settings (language) and then said: if the AI answers well from the docs, no tool is needed.
**How to apply:** no app-settings tool was built; the evidence says one would not have helped. Script: scratchpad `lang.py` pattern (grep person messages for language words). Related: [[app-guide-for-ai-and-people]], [[jusprin-chat-capture-design]].

name: history-trimming-by-size
description: 2026-10-15 5cf784d30b on local jusprin-newui (unpushed) - chat history to the model trimmed by a 64 KiB budget in three stages; kHistoryMessages (20 entries) is gone.
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project

  modified: 2026-10-16T03:15:22.605Z
---

`AgentHost::make_agent_request` no longer keeps "the last 20 entries". The history has a 64 KiB budget, measured as the serialized entries, and is trimmed only when over it. Three stages, each stopping once the history fits: results of calls older than the last two assistant turns become the "not repeated here; call the tool again" note, oldest first; then whole calls are dropped, oldest first; then the oldest words, never the newest message. A turn means the assistant messages that share one `in_reply_to`.

The budget comes from 12 live 3-turn chats (model-nature-probe transcripts), which replayed at 9 to 33 KB with no result over 10 KB. Tests are in tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp, tagged `[history]`. The untracked report is report-history-trimming.md in worktree nice-morse-0dfae8.

**Why:** the old cut dropped the person's words while 16 KiB tool payloads stayed, and could send about 320 KiB.
**How to apply:** older memories that mention the 20-entry cap, such as [[printer-chat-tool-history-replay]], are stale on that point. Whether the model actually calls a tool again when it sees the note has not been measured live.

import pickle,collections as C,statistics as st

R=[x for v in ch.values() for x in v]
allR=[x for x in pickle.load(open('R.pkl','rb')) if x['user']!='263741']
TOT=sum(x['cost'] for x in allR)
def wtok(x): return x['w5']+x['w1']+x['wu']
def wrate(x):
    w=wtok(x); return (x['c_w']*1e6/w) if w else 4.0
# 1) shrink history when it passes C tokens to K tokens
def shrink(Cap,K):
    actual=sim=0; events=0
    for v in ch.values():
        s=0; prev=None
        for x in v:
            actual+=x['cost']
            g=x['prompt'] if prev is None else max(0,x['prompt']-prev['prompt'])
            s+=g; extra=0
            if s>Cap:
                events+=1; extra=(s*0.10+4000*10+2000*2)/1e6  # summary request: read history, write ~4k summary
                s=K+g
                new=s  # whole shrunk prompt written fresh
            else:
                new=min(wtok(x),s)
            reads=max(0,s-new-x['i'])
            sim+=x['c_i']+reads*0.10/1e6+new*wrate(x)/1e6+x['c_o']+extra

    return actual,sim,events
for Cap,K in [(100e3,40e3),(150e3,50e3),(200e3,70e3),(300e3,100e3)]:

# 2) 5-minute cache instead of 1-hour
a=s=0; band=C.Counter()
for v in ch.values():
    prev=None
    for x in v:
        a+=x['cost']; w=wtok(x)
        gap=None if prev is None else (x['ts']-prev['ts']).total_seconds()
        c=x['c_i']+x['c_o']+w*2.5/1e6
        if gap is not None and 300<gap<=3600:
            c+=x['cr']*2.5/1e6; band['5-60 min pause']+=1
        else: c+=x['cr']*0.10/1e6
        s+=c; prev=x
print('5-minute cache for everything: saves $%.1f (%.1f%% of spend); requests after a 5-60 min pause: %d'%(a-s,100*(a-s)/TOT,band['5-60 min pause']))
# gap distribution between consecutive requests in a chat
gaps=[(x['ts']-p['ts']).total_seconds() for v in ch.values() for p,x in zip(v,v[1:])]
for lo,hi in [(0,60),(60,300),(300,600),(600,1800),(1800,3600),(3600,1e9)]: print('  gap %5d-%5ds: %d'%(lo,min(hi,99999),sum(lo<g<=hi for g in gaps)))
# 3) pause >1h rewrites: cost of those requests and their size
p=[(x,(x['ts']-pv['ts']).total_seconds()) for v in ch.values() for pv,x in zip(v,v[1:]) if (x['ts']-pv['ts']).total_seconds()>3600]
print('resumed after >1h: %d requests, write cost $%.1f, median prompt %dk'%(len(p),sum(x['c_w'] for x,_ in p),st.median(x['prompt'] for x,_ in p)/1e3))
# 4) notes
notes=[x for x in allR if x['kind']=='note']; print('note requests %d cost $%.1f (%.0f%%), mean $%.3f'%(len(notes),sum(x['cost'] for x in notes),100*sum(x['cost'] for x in notes)/TOT,st.mean(x['cost'] for x in notes)))
EOF

content.text:
The biggest saving is in the app, not the model. Every time the AI uses a tool, the app attaches the whole workspace state to the result. Every later request in that chat then re-reads all of those copies. Removing the repeats would cut roughly 13–30% of the bill. That's my estimate, and it still needs a quality check.

**Where the money went (Nov 13–26, Sonnet 5.5, your own account left out)**
- Total $352 across 139 people and 10,391 requests. My daily figures match the Console where it was checked before, for example Nov 24 at $45.29. The days after Nov 18 haven't been checked against the Console.
- Writing to the cache is 59%, reading from it 28%, output 12%, uncached input 1%.
- It's concentrated: 45 chats (of 725) each reached a request over 200k tokens, and they cost half of all spend. The top 10 people cost 52%.
- Turns the app starts on its own, such as "the slice finished", cost 22%. People aren't charged credits for these.

**What fills the long chats**

I looked at the 30 largest chats the server keeps, plus 60 others spread across sizes. Tool results are 58% of the request text in the large chats. Most of each result is the workspace copy the app adds in [AgentHost.cpp:3559](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentHost.cpp:3559). Those copies are 46% of all request text in the large chats and 21% in the spread sample. About half of them are identical to the copy just before.

**Ways to cut cost (all proposals, savings estimated by replaying every chat's recorded requests)**
1. **Send the workspace in a tool result only when it changed, or only what changed:** about $45 (13%) for dropping only the identical copies, up to about $100 (30%) for dropping them all. The model reads the state from these copies, so this needs a test showing it still knows the state.
2. **Keep cached prompts 5 minutes instead of 1 hour:** saves about $20 (6%) gross. That's one constant in the gateway. An earlier, smaller sample said this breaks even once new chats lose the shared opening prompt sooner. That loss would take about $3–5 off. So I'd call it a measured trial.
3. **Shrink a chat's history once it passes about 150k tokens:** about $32 (9%). It costs the AI detail from earlier in the chat. The best moment is when someone comes back after more than an hour, because the whole prompt is written again then anyway. Those comebacks cost $41 (12%).
4. **Cache misses partway through a chat:** $15 (4%). Most come from retries and edited messages, which is expected. About $4 are full misses seconds apart within one turn, which I can't explain yet.

A cheaper model, such as Haiku 5.5 at a twentieth of Sonnet's price, is a quality trade-off for you to decide on with an eval, not a free saving.

**Decision needed:** which saving should I work on first? It's your call because the first two change what the AI sees, and both need an eval run that costs money. Option 1 saves the most and keeps the conversation intact, but changes a JusPrin tool contract. Option 2 is a one-line gateway change you could watch for a week, worth about 4–6%. I'd start with option 1. Should I start with the workspace copies, or try the 5-minute cache first?

Yes, all four could be done in the gateway, but they differ in how cleanly.

1. **Workspace copies in tool results: yes, with one catch.** The app sends the whole chat with every request, and the gateway already edits request bodies before forwarding them (it sets the cache lifetime that way). It could replace a workspace copy that's identical to the one before it with a short marker such as "unchanged since the previous result". Three things make this work or limit it:
   - The edit depends only on earlier messages, so every request gets the same edit. The cache keeps working, and Anthropic never sees an edited history, because the model only ever saw the shortened version.
   - It helps people on older app versions right away, with no app release.
   - The catch: the gateway would depend on the app's tool-result format, a JSON object with a `workspace` field. If the app changes that format, the saving stops without any error. A test in the gateway against a recorded request would catch that.

   Sending only the changed fields, instead of dropping identical copies, could also be done in the gateway, but it's a bigger edit to tool results.

2. **5-minute cache: yes, fully.** It's the `CACHE_TTL` constant in `upstream.py`.

3. **Shrinking long histories: yes, but not as compaction.** Anthropic's server-side compaction needs the client to send back the summary blocks it returns, and the app re-sends its own history, so the gateway would have to store state for every chat. The fit for a pass-through gateway is Anthropic's context editing, which clears old tool results on Anthropic's side before the model reads them, with no state to keep. Two things I haven't verified:
   - whether it works with Sonnet 5.5's rules on editing past history, and
   - how much cache it gives up each time it clears.

   The model also may not know why the old results are gone and may call those tools again.

4. **The unexplained cache misses: the diagnosis can be done in the gateway, the fix probably not.** The gateway can send Anthropic's cache-diagnosis header, which reports why each miss happened. The cause is most likely something the app changes partway through a turn, so the fix would probably be in the app.

Choosing a cheaper model is also a gateway setting (the alias config), though it's a quality decision, not a free saving.

The gateway only sees JusPrin Cloud traffic. That's fine here, because people using their own API key pay their own bills.

202-- `input_tokens` - just the tail after the last breakpoint
203-
204:If `cache_creation_input_tokens` is instead near the full conversation size on every request, either the prefix is being rewritten upstream of the breakpoint, or the write is happening for a reason payload diffing and cache diagnostics can't localize - with thinking enabled on a model that strips prior-turn thinking blocks the invalidation is server-side (§ Invalidation hierarchy), and a single turn that appends more than 20 positions (parallel tool-call runs collapse to one position - § 20-block lookback window) pushes the previous entry out of the lookback so every request rewrites the whole conversation with byte-identical payloads (§ 20-block lookback window). Rule both show-nothing cases out first from the model and the turn shape. Reads can only land on positions where a previous request wrote a breakpoint, so the usage fields say *that* the prefix broke (reads collapse, often to zero) but not where - the payload diff or cache diagnostics below localizes the exact point.
205-
206:**Finding the invalidator.** Log several consecutive request payloads (the full JSON body) and diff adjacent pairs. In a growing conversation, adjacent payloads legitimately differ at the end (the newly appended turn); what must be byte-identical is the overlap - the previous request's prompt should reappear unchanged as a prefix of the next. Strip `cache_control` markers before diffing: the moving marker always differs between adjacent requests and is not an invalidator (previously-marked blocks are still cache hits). The first remaining divergence inside the overlapping region is the invalidation point. This catches the class of bug code review misses - nondeterministic serialization, a library reordering keys or fields, a value that changes between requests but not within one. On the Claude API, cache diagnostics (beta header `cache-diagnosis-2026-04-07`) does this comparison server-side once you opt in: send the header on **every** request - fingerprints are stored only for requests that carried it, so a one-shot retrofit fails with `previous_message_not_found` - then pass the previous response's `id` as `diagnostics.previous_message_id` and the response's `diagnostics` object names where the two requests diverged (model, system, tools, or message history). No payload logging needed. Availability: `shared/platform-availability.md`.
207-
208-**Unexplained writes:** `usage.cache_creation` breaks `cache_creation_input_tokens` down by TTL (`ephemeral_5m_input_tokens` / `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`). Server tools such as web search automatically insert a 5-minute cache write after tool results when the request already uses caching - writes at a position you didn't mark; expected behavior, not an invalidator.
209-
210----
211-
212-## Invalidation hierarchy
213-
214-Not every parameter change invalidates everything. The API has three cache tiers, and changes only invalidate their own tier and below:
215-
216-| Change | Tools cache | System cache | Messages cache |
217-|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
218-| Tool definitions (add/remove/reorder) | No | No | No |
219-| Model switch | No | No | No |
220-| `speed`, web-search, citations toggle | Yes | No | No |
221-| System prompt content | Yes | No | No |
222-| `tool_choice`, images | Yes | Yes | No |
223-| `thinking` or `effort` change | model-specific | model-specific | No |
224-| Message content | Yes | Yes | No |
225-
226-Implication: you can change `tool_choice` per-request without losing the tools+system cache, and message-content changes never touch it. Thinking and `effort` changes always invalidate the messages cache, and on models that render the thinking configuration ahead of tools and system they invalidate those caches too - pin thinking and effort settings per route rather than varying them per request. Only tool-definition and model changes force a full rebuild on every model.
227-
228-**Three of these rows have a cache-preserving escape hatch** - the tools row, the system-prompt row, and (on Claude Fable 5.2 / Claude Mythos 5.2 / Claude Fable 5.1 / Claude Mythos 5.1 / Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Opus 5 / Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Claude Haiku 5.5) the `effort` row - each by moving the change out of the top-level request and into a system message inside `messages[]`, after the cached prefix. The inject-then-delete reminder pattern has its own hatch: a text block appended after the `tool_result` blocks in the user message, never deleted. **Availability differs per row** - they are not gated together:
229-
230-| Top-level change that invalidates | Cache-preserving form | Available on |
231-|---|---|---|
232-| Tool definitions (add/remove) | `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` blocks - see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` § Mid-conversation tool changes | Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Fable 5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5 (not Claude Sonnet 5), behind `mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01` or `inline-tools-2026-09-15` |
233-| System prompt content | A `{"role": "system", "content": "..."}` message - see § Mid-conversation system messages above | Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Fable 5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, no beta header |
234-| Per-turn reminder (inject, then delete next request) | A turn-scoped `clear_at: "next_user_message"` system message, left in the transcript - see § Mid-conversation system messages above (without the beta: a text block after the `tool_result` blocks, earlier copies kept) | Same models as mid-conversation system messages, behind `mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21` |
235-| `effort` change | A `{"role": "system", "content": [], "output_config": {"effort": ...}}` message - see `shared/model-migration.md` -> Migrating to Claude Fable 5.1 from Claude Fable 5 | Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 (thinking on only), behind `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01` |
236-| Dropped thinking blocks (a Claude Fable 5.2 / Claude Mythos 5.2 / Claude Fable 5.1 / Claude Mythos 5.1 / Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Claude Haiku 5.5 block replayed to a model that can't read it - no model released earlier reads Claude Fable 5.2's or Claude Mythos 5.2's, and `shared/model-migration.md` says who reads the others' - or a history-editing-check `drop_block`) | None - the API drops the block on that request and the messages cache changes from its position onward; tools and system caches are intact. Blocks the receiving model can read, passed back unchanged, keep the cache intact | - |
237-
238-Model switch has no escape hatch: caches are model-scoped. Keep the main loop on one model and spawn a subagent for cheaper sub-tasks (see `agent-design.md` § Caching for Agents).
239-
240-**Thinking blocks and the messages cache (model-specific).** On Claude Fable 5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.2, Mythos Preview, Opus 4.5 and later (Claude Opus 5.5 included), Sonnet 4.6 and later, and Claude Haiku 5.5, previous-turn thinking blocks are preserved by default, so passing a regular (non-tool-result) user message with thinking enabled leaves the messages cache valid. On earlier Opus and Sonnet models and Haiku models through Haiku 4.5, that same request strips previously-cached thinking blocks from context, and every message after the first stripped block falls out of cache - in an agent loop this shows up as a `cache_creation_input_tokens` spike on turns where a plain user message follows tool use. (Toggling thinking on/off between requests is a separate, all-models invalidator of the messages cache - see the hierarchy table above. Changing `output_config.effort` behaves the same as changing thinking parameters; setting the model's default effort explicitly is equivalent to omitting it, so pinning the default costs nothing.)
241-
242----
243-
244-## 20-block lookback window
245-
246-Each breakpoint walks backward **at most 20 positions** to find a prior cache entry. On the Claude API a run of consecutive `tool_use` blocks counts as one position, and so does a run of consecutive `tool_result` blocks, so a turn with many *parallel* tool calls doesn't push the previous request's entry out of the window; a turn that adds more than 20 positions of other content (long sequential tool loops, many text/image blocks) still can - the next request's breakpoint won't find the previous cache and silently misses.

  1. **Beta header:** The page never names an `anthropic-beta` value for cache diagnostics. Its raw cURL examples send only `anthropic-version: 2026-10-21`. The SDK examples use `client.beta.messages.create(...)`, and the cURL examples post to `/v1/messages`. The page says the set of active `anthropic-beta` headers is a prompt-affecting parameter, so changing it produces `unavailable`. Required on every request: the docs say "Include the `diagnostics` object on every turn," and the API stores a fingerprint only for requests that include it.
  
  2. **Request field:** A top-level `diagnostics` object with `previous_message_id`.
     - First turn: `"diagnostics": {"previous_message_id": null}`
     - Later turns: `"diagnostics": {"previous_message_id": "<id from previous response>"}`
     - Yes, it is the response `id` (`msg_...`). The docs say "include the previous response's `id` as `diagnostics.previous_message_id`," and the example id is `msg_01Xyz...`.
  
  3. **Where the diagnosis appears:**
     - Non-streamed: a `diagnostics` field on the Message object.
     - Streamed: the docs say "`diagnostics` appears on the `message_start` event." The SDK examples read it from the event's embedded message (`start.Message.Diagnostics`, `event.message->diagnostics`). The docs give no SSE JSON for this event, so the wrapper shape is inferred, not documented.
     - Allowed values:
       - `null`: no `diagnostics` object sent, `previous_message_id` was `null`, or nothing diverged before the last breakpoint.
       - `{"cache_miss_reason": null}`: comparison still running when serialized. Treat as inconclusive.
       - `{"cache_miss_reason": {...}}`: `type` is one of `model_changed`, `system_changed`, `tools_changed`, `messages_changed`, `previous_message_not_found`, `unavailable`.
     - Fields: `type`, plus `cache_missed_input_tokens` (an integer) on the four `*_changed` types only. The docs describe it as "an estimate of how many input tokens fell after the divergence point" and say it is "a magnitude indicator rather than a billing number."
     - The divergence location is the `type` itself (`model`, `system`, `tools`, `messages`). There are no index or reason fields.
     - The docs say the response "reports the earliest divergence only."
  
  4. **Pricing, latency, caching, limits:**
     - Pricing and latency: the docs state no cost or latency effect for diagnostics. They say the comparison is about request structure "independent of whether the cache actually hit," and that diagnostics "never blocks or fails your request."
     - Retention: fingerprints are kept for "a short period" or "a limited time." No duration is given.
     - Scope: the previous request must be in the same organization and workspace, or the result is `previous_message_not_found`. On the Claude API, compare the `anthropic-workspace-id` response header. The docs do not say whether the same API key is required.
     - 1-hour and 5-minute TTLs: the diagnostics page does not mention TTL. The prompt-caching page says `"cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h" }` is supported, and that "a 1-hour cache entry must appear before any 5-minute cache entries."

     - Thinking: the `unavailable` type covers a differing `thinking` parameter. The caching page says changing the thinking configuration invalidates message blocks.
     - Web search: the caching page says toggling web search "modifies the system prompt," so it would invalidate the system cache. The docs do not state what diagnostics reports for it; `system_changed` is my inference.

The request still runs: diagnostics "never blocks or fails your request." No error status is documented, so you should expect success.
  
  6. **Availability:**
     - Platforms: Claude API (stable) and Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) (stable). Managed Agents: not available.
     - Models: the docs say "Cache diagnostics are available on every model." The page's `supportedModels` list is: claude-fable-5-2, claude-mythos-5-2, claude-fable-5-1, claude-mythos-5-1, claude-fable-5, claude-mythos-5, claude-mythos-preview, claude-opus-5-5, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-haiku-5-5, claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, claude-opus-4-8, claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-6, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-5-20251101, claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929.

    "id": "msg_01Xyz...",
    "type": "message",
    "role": "assistant",

are rewritten; every other event keeps its fields as upstream sent them (line
endings are normalised to \\n). An event that says the reply failed is never
forwarded: EventRewriter.failure names it, and the gateway answers instead.
"""
import json
from typing import AsyncIterator, Dict, List, Optional

# The events that end a reply that did not fail.
FINAL_EVENTS = {'anthropic': {'message_stop'}, 'responses': {'response.completed', 'response.incomplete'}}


class EventRewriter:
    """Rewrites one stream's events for the client and collects token usage."""

    def __init__(self, fmt: str, alias_id: str):
        self.fmt = fmt
        self.alias_id = alias_id
        self.usage: Dict[str, int] = {}
        self.finished = False  # the reply's final event has gone through
        self.last_event = None  # the type of the last event rewritten

    def failure(self, lines: List[str]) -> Optional[dict]:
        """The event, as the provider sent it, when it says the reply failed;
        None otherwise."""
        data = _data(lines)
        if not isinstance(data, dict):

        kind = data.get('type')

            return data
        return None

    def rewrite(self, lines: List[str]) -> bytes:
        data = _data(lines)

            self.last_event = data.get('type')
            self.finished = self.finished or self.last_event in FINAL_EVENTS[self.fmt]
            if self._rewrite(data):
                kept = [line for line in lines if not line.startswith('data:')]
                lines = kept + ['data: ' + json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',', ':'))]
        return ('\n'.join(lines) + '\n\n').encode()

    def _rewrite(self, data: dict) -> bool:
        """Edits data in place; True when anything changed."""

            user = await sync_to_async(_authenticate_scope, thread_sensitive=True)(scope)
            if user is None:
                raise GatewayError(401, 'unauthorized')
            headers = _headers(scope)
            turn_id = headers.get('x-jusprin-turn', '')
            request_kind = headers.get('x-jusprin-request', '')
            chat_id = headers.get('x-jusprin-chat')
            facts.update(user_id=user.id, turn_id=turn_id, request_kind=request_kind, chat_id=chat_id,
                         app=headers.get('user-agent'), request_bytes=headers.get('content-length'))
            if not TURN_ID.match(turn_id):
                raise GatewayError(400, 'invalid_request', 'The X-JusPrin-Turn header is missing or not valid.')
            if request_kind not in REQUEST_KINDS:
                raise GatewayError(400, 'invalid_request', 'The X-JusPrin-Request header must be reply, title or note.')
            if chat_id is not None and not capture.CHAT_ID.match(chat_id):
                raise GatewayError(400, 'invalid_request', 'The X-JusPrin-Chat header must be 32 lowercase hex digits.')
            large = await stack.enter_async_context(_large_request_slot(scope))
            raw_body = await _read_body(receive, settings.JUSPRIN_V2_MAX_BODY_BYTES)
            if raw_body is None:
                return  # the client left before sending the whole body
            if large or len(raw_body) > settings.JUSPRIN_V2_LARGE_BODY_BYTES:
                # Parsing and re-encoding megabytes of JSON takes long enough
                # to stall every websocket this process serves.
                upstream = await asyncio.to_thread(prepare, self.fmt, raw_body, get_aliases(), user.id)
            else:
                upstream = prepare(self.fmt, raw_body, get_aliases(), user.id)
            del raw_body
            facts.update(alias=upstream.alias.id, upstream_model=upstream.backend.model, effort=upstream.effort)
            try:
                admission = await sync_to_async(admit, thread_sensitive=True)(
                    user.id, turn_id, request_kind, upstream.alias, chat_id)
            except CreditsExhausted as e:
                raise credits_exhausted(e.cost, e.balance, e.details())
            if admission is Admission.RATE_LIMITED:
                raise GatewayError(429, 'rate_limited')
            # The chat's title as the app shows it, percent-encoded UTF-8, so
            # Billing and usage can name the chat; optional, and older apps
            # don't send it. The app encodes it, so one that is not UTF-8 is
            # unexpected.
            title = headers.get('x-jusprin-chat-title')
            if chat_id is not None and title:
                await sync_to_async(remember_chat_title, thread_sensitive=True)(

        except GatewayError as e:
            # A request the app sent that this server refuses is ours: the app
            # is on the other end.
            if e.code in ('invalid_request', 'unknown_model'):

content.thinking:
I'm wiring up a diagnosis step in gateway.py: for the anthropic format, on non-title requests with a chat id, I'll look up the previous message id off the event loop and pass it into a diagnosis dict, which goes to both prepare calls. I also need the turn object to carry a diagnosed flag and chat key, and to call remember() after the relay.

I'm also going to store the message id in Redis under a per-user, per-chat key with a 2-hour TTL, using the BREDIS helper. Langfuse metadata gets a cache_miss_reason entry pulled from the rewriter diagnostics, set to None when there was no diagnosis. Titles are excluded from this, and the Langfuse usage docstring needs updating too.

content.text:
Both gateway changes are written and pass every JusPrin 2 server test. They're in the worktree `/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise/.claude/worktrees/cache-5m-diagnosis`, on branch `claude/cache-5m-diagnosis`, and nothing is committed or deployed. Neither change alters what the AI reads, so neither needs a quality check before it ships.

**5-minute cache**

`CACHE_TTL` in `upstream.py` is now `'5m'`. My replay of the last 14 days estimates a saving of about 5%. Langfuse already prices 5-minute cache writes at $2.50 per million tokens, so its costs stay correct after the switch.

**Cache-miss diagnosis**

Each chat request now tells Anthropic which earlier response it follows. Anthropic then says whether the cache missed, and why. It names what changed first (the model, the system prompt, the tools or the messages) and estimates how many tokens missed. In detail:
- Title requests and requests from apps that don't send a chat id ask nothing, because they have prompts of their own.
- The gateway keeps each chat's newest response id in Redis for 2 hours, so the next request can name it.
- The reason is logged in Langfuse as `cache_miss_reason` and removed from the reply before it reaches the app.
- I sent three tiny requests to Anthropic with the production key, the same `anthropic-version` and the beta header the gateway will send. They cost about 3 cents. The reason arrives where the docs say, and it named "system prompt changed" on the request where I changed it.

All 367 JusPrin 2 server tests pass, including new ones for:
- the first request in a chat naming no earlier response,
- the next request naming the one before,
- separate chats, title requests and DeepSeek requests,
- the reason being logged and kept out of the app's reply,
- the beta header joining any the backend already sends.

**Does the workspace change need testing first?**

Yes. Unlike the two changes above, it changes what the AI reads. The risk is that the AI loses track of the current state, or calls the workspace tool more often, which costs more requests.

We can test it without real users. The server keeps 757 complete chats. I'd take about 100 points from them and rebuild each request twice, once as sent and once with the repeated copies replaced. Then I'd run both versions and compare what the AI does next and what it says about the current state. At today's prices that's roughly $20–40. Running it would need your yes on the budget.

Should I commit both gateway changes to master and push, or not yet?

content.text:
Not for this test. Your subscription could pay for the requests, but it can't send them the way the test needs.

**What a subscription covers.** Anthropic's help article says that `claude -p` (Claude Code run from a script) and the Agent SDK draw from your plan's usage limits when you're signed in with a Claude plan. Plain Messages API requests, which is what the JusPrin gateway sends, aren't covered.

**Why that breaks the test.** The test only means something if each request is exactly what the app sent: JusPrin's system prompt, its tools, and the chat history with every tool call and result, once as sent and once with the repeated workspace copies replaced. `claude -p` and the Agent SDK run Claude Code's own setup around every request. They can take a custom system prompt and custom tools, but they can't take a ready-made history that already holds tool calls and results. I'd have to flatten each chat into plain text, and that would measure something other than what the app sends.

**Something worth checking.** The same article has an update dated October 7, 2026, saying Max, Ultra and Team plans now include monthly API credits. If yours has them and they apply to plain API requests, they might pay for the test. I haven't verified how those credits are used. You can check your account on the Claude Console.

**Decision needed:** should I run the workspace-copy test on the API with the production key, capped at $40? It's your call because it spends money. It replays about 100 points from the kept chats, each sent once as it was and once with repeated copies replaced, and compares what the AI does next and what it says about the current state. Skipping it means either shipping the change untested or not shipping it. I'd run it. Run it with a $40 cap, or not now?

Yes, it can run there, and it would cost about a dollar instead of $20–40. But it wouldn't answer the question that matters.

**Why DeepSeek alone isn't enough.** Of the 10,826 gateway requests since launch, 97% went to Sonnet 5.5, the Expert model, and almost all the spend is there. If DeepSeek passes, that doesn't mean Sonnet would. If DeepSeek fails, it might just be DeepSeek being weaker at following state. There's also a format gap. The kept chats with the long histories are Sonnet chats in Anthropic's request format, and DeepSeek goes through OpenRouter in a different format. I'd have to convert every request, and the conversion changes it, for example by dropping Sonnet's thinking blocks.

**Where DeepSeek is useful:**
- **To debug the test itself.** Picking the 100 points, rebuilding each request twice and comparing the answers all have to work before the results mean anything. Running that on DeepSeek first means bugs in my test cost cents, not Sonnet prices.
- **For the Standard tier.** The gateway change would apply to DeepSeek requests too, so a DeepSeek result is a real answer for the people who use the Standard model.

**Decision needed:** should I build and debug the test on DeepSeek first (about $1), then run the real comparison on Sonnet 5.5 with the production key, capped at $40? content.text:
You're right. I sized the test around "does the AI still behave well in general", when the change is small and most of what can go wrong with it can be checked for free.

**What the change does (proposed, not built).** When a tool result's workspace copy is byte-for-byte the same as the copy in the tool result before it, the gateway swaps it for the words "unchanged since the previous result". No information goes missing: the identical copy is still in the request, a few blocks earlier. The AI also gets a full workspace snapshot at the start of every turn.

**What it could break, and the cheapest way to check each:**
1. **It mangles a request:** bad JSON, the wrong block edited, or a tool result that isn't JSON. *Free:* run the change over all 757 kept chats. Check that the output is valid, that only workspace fields changed, and that every swapped copy really equals the one before it. Anything unexpected is left as it is.
2. **It breaks the cache and costs more.** *Free:* cutting a kept chat at an earlier message gives the request the app sent at that point. Apply the change at every such cut and check that each result is an exact prefix of the next. After the deploy, the new cache-miss reason in Langfuse shows the same thing on live traffic.
3. **It saves less than I claimed.** *Measured just now, free:* I ran Anthropic's token counter on 89 kept chats with and without the swap. It cut prompt tokens by 20% in the 30 largest chats and 10% in a spread of 60. Since the long chats carry most of the cost, that's about 12% of the bill, roughly $40 over the last 14 days.
4. **The AI misreads the marker and loses track of the state.** This is the only behavior risk. *About $2:* pick 5 points that come right after a swapped copy, where the next step depends on the state. Send Sonnet each point with and without the swap, and compare what it does next.
5. **Something only real use shows.** *Free:* switch it on for a share of people. The gateway already splits people into groups by user id. Compare a few days of workspace-tool calls per turn, requests per turn and cost per message between the two groups.

A bigger replay is only needed if step 4 or step 5 shows a difference. If the AI does the same thing in all 5 cases and the live numbers hold, I'd stop there.

**Decision needed:** should I build the change in the gateway, run checks 1 and 2 on the kept chats, then send the 5 live cases (about $2 with the production key)? It's your call because the live cases spend money and the change alters what the AI reads. Offline checks only costs nothing, but leaves the one behavior risk unchecked until real people meet it. I'd do both. Build and check everything, or offline checks only?

1344:Claude Fable 5.1 is the previous Fable release - for the most demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. **Claude Mythos 5.1** (`claude-mythos-5-1`) has the same capabilities and pricing and is available only to organizations verified through Anthropic's verification programs, such as the Cyber Verification Program. Everything in this section applies to both models except where § Claude Mythos 5.1 below says otherwise (who the history-editing check is enforced for, platform availability, and safeguards that depend on the access program). Verified organizations moving from Mythos Preview to Claude Mythos 5.1 use `claude-mythos-5-1`; everyone else targeting Claude Fable 5.1 uses `claude-fable-5-1`. 1M token context window by default (the maximum is also the default), up to 128K output tokens per request.

1635:### Breaking change 3: thinking blocks are preserved only in the conversation that produced them
1637:The published docs file this and breaking change 2 together under *preserved thinking*; this one is the history-editing check (the docs' prefix check, the API reference's conversation check) - editing earlier turns invalidates every later thinking block. The API field names for it say `prefix_mismatch_behavior` / `prefix_binding_mismatch` - the same check. Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 both run it ("Who is enforced" below).
1641:A Claude Fable 5.1 thinking block's `signature` also records the conversation prefix that produced it - the top-level `system` prompt, the set of tools in `tools`, and every message before the block (with server-side compaction, the prefix starts at the most recent compaction block) - plus a chain to the previous thinking block across turns (earlier thinking blocks aren't part of the prefix, but each block records the one before it, which is why blocks can be removed from the *front* of the history and not from the middle). When the transcript comes back, the API checks that this prefix is unchanged. Claude Code, claude.ai, Managed Agents, and the Agent SDK keep the prefix intact for you; **if your code builds the `messages` array itself, check it before migrating** (the three-step check is below). **Who is enforced:** on Claude Fable 5.1, new accounts **created on or after August 31, 2026**, on every platform. Enforcement scope is decided per model - Claude Opus 5.5 also enforces it for new accounts only, while on Claude Mythos 5.1 it is enforced by default whatever the account's age, on the Claude API, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry - so make your application compatible regardless of your account's age: the same patterns keep the prompt cache warm, and you can test against the check from any account by sending `prefix_mismatch_behavior`. On models that enforce new accounts only, for accounts created earlier the API *records* the mismatch but acts on it only when the request sets `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior` - **any value, including `"error"`, opts the request into enforcement**, which is also how you test from an older organization (the beta header alone does not opt in: it lets you set the field and, on a request that leaves the field unset, lists each failing block in `input_transformations` as `thinking_mismatch_allowed` while the model still receives it). If you ship a tool or framework that people run with their own API key, test with the field set: your users on new organizations are enforced before you are. To see whether your own organization is enforced by default on a model, send that model a request that edits history without the beta header - a 400 that names the header means it is. Platform note: the opt-in controls (the beta header, `prefix_mismatch_behavior`, `input_transformations`) are available under the same beta name on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Cloud Vertex AI (Claude in Amazon Bedrock: the `anthropic-beta` header; Bedrock's InvokeModel API: the `anthropic_beta` body field; Vertex: the `anthropic-beta` HTTP header - the SDKs' `betas` parameter does the right thing on each); Microsoft Foundry is unconfirmed. Wherever an endpoint rejects the header or the beta name, the opt-in test path doesn't apply and recovery is strip-and-retry (`shared/platform-availability.md` has the matrix).
1653:**Where the check is enforced, a request that replays an invalidated block is rejected** with a 400 `invalid_request_error`, decided before any output. Retrying the same body fails the same way; the token-counting endpoint runs the same check. (In the Message Batches API the *unset* default drops failing blocks instead of failing the item - set `"error"` explicitly if you want batch items to error.)
1656:messages.5.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block. The block is bound to a different conversation. Remove the block, or set `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior` to "drop_block". That setting requires the `thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01` value in the `anthropic-beta` header.
1659:The last sentence appears only when the request didn't send the beta header; the message can end with one more sentence naming the first message that changed - the actionable diagnostic. (A tampered or undecryptable signature is a different failure: the same leading clause with *no* "bound to a different conversation" sentence, always a 400, and `prefix_mismatch_behavior` doesn't apply.) 1673:`thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior` takes `"error"` or `"drop_block"`. On an enforced account the default is `"error"` with or without the header (the header only lets you set the field, and adds `input_transformations` to responses). On an account that isn't enforced, an unset field lets failing blocks through to the model, and with the header each one is listed in `input_transformations` as an entry of type `thinking_mismatch_allowed`. In the Message Batches API the unset default on an enforced account drops the failing blocks instead of failing the item; a Batches item fails as `errored` only with `prefix_mismatch_behavior: "error"` set. # Global Claude Code Rules

## How to Communicate

Talk like a colleague explaining something out loud, not like a report.

1. **Full sentences, one idea each.** Lead with a concrete case (someone opens a file, chats twenty times, then runs out of credits) before any general point. Never pack a mechanism into a noun phrase like "hidden fair-use ceiling". Say what the person sees happen, step by step.

2. **No labels of your own.** Names you made up while working ("phase 2", "board 6a", "the M4 batch", "the three decisions") mean nothing to me. Name a thing by what it is or does. To ask about a screen, say where it is and send the picture.

3. **Ask decisions in full, as questions.** Start with "Decision needed". Give one paragraph per decision: what it is, why it's mine, the options with what each costs, and your pick. End it with a "?". Never refer to a decision by a label, a count, or the report it's in. Don't hand me a choice you could settle yourself by searching or measuring.

4. **Mark proposals as proposals.** Keep apart what the code does today, what you propose, and what I have agreed to. Never write an idea I haven't approved as if it were settled. Before calling something "my rule", find my actual words.

5. **Report outcomes, not the journey.** Leave out problems you hit and solved unless they change what I do next. For an investigation, say what the problem was, how you solved it, what you tested and the result, and what's still open. Keep it under about 500 words.

## Git Commit Policy

When the user asks to commit changes:

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` to review the changes.
2. If you are confident that both the changes are correct and the proposed commit message accurately describes them, proceed with git commit without asking for confirmation.
3. If you have any uncertainty about either, stop and ask the user for explicit confirmation before committing.

When the user asks to revert or amend commits:
1. Explain what will be reverted/amended
2. Ask for confirmation before executing any `git revert`, `git reset`, or `git commit --amend` commands
3. Only proceed after explicit user approval
4. Never revert commits without explicit user confirmation.

This applies to all git operations that modify commit history.

## Submodule Policy

**Never commit or attempt to commit submodule updates.**

When `git status` shows modified submodules (e.g., `modified: some-submodule (new commits)`):
- Do not stage or commit the submodule change
- Do not include submodules when running `git add`
- Leave submodule management to the user

## Testing Principles

1. Always test your code change unless the change is not testable.

2. If the change is not testable, highlight the reason why it's not testable to get the user's attention.

3. By default, do end-to-end testing on everything that may potentially be impacted by your change on the local dev environment.

4. Search for how the dev environment should be started if it's not obvious.

5. Look for README files in the project for related info.

6. Check if the local dev is already running before you try to start it again.

## Software Engineering Principles

1. **Don't reinvent the wheel (avoid Not Invented Here).** Before building anything, check whether the codebase or the libraries it already uses do it, and reuse that. Re-implementing something is a decision that needs a stated justification.

## Where to Create Worktrees and Temporary Folders

This file is read by more than one coding tool, so each rule names the idea first and the tool-specific path second.

1. **Use the location your own tool already uses for worktrees.** Claude Code: `<repo>/.claude/worktrees/`. Codex: `~/.codex/worktrees/`. If this session was started inside a worktree the tool created, put any further worktree beside it.
2. **Never create a worktree or a working folder in `~` or directly under `~/Projects`.** That includes sibling folders such as `<repo>-worktrees`. This holds for a different repo than the one the session started in: use that repo's tool-managed location (rule 1) or the scratch directory (rule 3).
3. **Short-lived worktrees, build output, logs, screenshots and scripts go in the session's scratch or temp directory** if the tool gives one (Claude Code names it in the session instructions). If it gives none, use a new folder under the system temp directory, not the home directory.
4. **Keep non-worktree files out of worktree folders.** Logs, screenshots and scripts do not belong beside the worktrees. They go in the scratch directory, or inside the one worktree they concern.
5. **Use absolute paths when creating a worktree.** A shell may reset its working directory between commands, and a path starting with `~` or `..` can land somewhere unintended.
6. **Say where it is.** After creating a worktree, tell the user its full path, and remove it and its branch when the work is finished and merged.

## Bug Fix Policy

**Never apply a fix for a bug you cannot reproduce.**

Before writing any fix:
1. Reproduce the bug first in the local dev environment.
2. If the bug cannot be reproduced locally (e.g., only manifests in release mode, requires specific device conditions, or the debug framework masks the crash), stop and tell the user — do not apply the fix.
3. A fix is only valid if you can demonstrate the broken behavior before the fix and the correct behavior after.

## Epistemic Discipline — Root Cause of Repeated Errors

**The core failure mode: confusing "generating a plausible explanation" with "knowing the answer."**

Coherent ≠ true. A narrative that feels right because it's internally consistent is not a verified fact.

Rules to follow every time:

1. **Search before asserting, not after being challenged.** The internet is always available. Use it proactively, not reactively as damage control.

2. **Explicitly label inference vs. verified fact.** If it hasn't been confirmed by a source, say "my hypothesis is..." or "I'd expect..." — never state it as fact.

3. **"I don't know yet" is a complete and correct answer.** Saying it is more helpful than fabricating a confident-sounding explanation.

## Problem Definition Before Search

**A well-defined problem statement is more valuable than a clever hypothesis.**

The discipline:
1. **Define the problem precisely first.** Strip out assumptions one by one until the statement contains only what is actually known. Remove irrelevant context (e.g. subscription type if it doesn't affect the symptom).
2. **Search for the problem directly** — not for your hypothesis. People who already solved the same problem will surface the real root cause.
3. **Let the search results form the conclusion.** Don't search to confirm what you already believe.
4. **Be flexible about scope.** Start with the most likely affected area (e.g. Discord) but stay open to other channels or systems being equally or more affected.

Searching to validate a hypothesis finds confirmation of whatever you already believed. Searching for the problem finds answers.


## GCP / kubectl Credential Policy

Always use the service account `ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com` for all `gcloud` and `kubectl` operations. Before running any such command, switch to it:

```bash
gcloud config set account ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

The personal account `k@obico.io` is reserved for the user's own interactive CLI use and its OAuth tokens expire — do not rely on it.

## Sentry Access

- Instance: `sentry.obico.io`
- API base: `https://sentry.obico.io/api/0/`
- Auth token: `REDACTED`
- Usage: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" <api_url>`

# CLAUDE.md

JusPrin — a long-lived fork of OrcaSlicer (open-source C++17 3D slicer, wxWidgets GUI, CMake build system).

## Upstream vs. fork attribution

This checkout holds two codebases: upstream OrcaSlicer (the `upstream` remote, SoftFever/OrcaSlicer) and the JusPrin fork's changes on top of it. Fork changes include everything under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the seams the fork added inside OrcaSlicer-owned files.

- Say "OrcaSlicer does X" only for behavior upstream ships. Behavior added by a fork commit is "JusPrin does X", even when it lives in an OrcaSlicer-owned file.
- Check before attributing; the file path is not enough. Run `git blame` on the line, then `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'`. No upstream branch containing the commit means the fork owns it. Run `git fetch upstream` first if the remote may be stale.
- If you have not checked, say it is unverified whether the behavior is upstream or fork.

## Branches

- `jusprin-dev` is the development branch. Start each change on a new branch from it and land the change there. It began at `975c703f08`, the merge of OrcaSlicer 2.5.0, and contains the earlier development branches `jusprin-newui` and `ui-walkthrough`; start nothing new on those.
- `main` is the stable branch and GitHub's default branch: the repository's front page, its issue forms, and the workflows GitHub runs on a schedule come from it.
  - Never force-push `main`, so that people who cloned the repository never have to force-pull. Only in an extreme case with no other way out, and with Kenneth's yes, may an admin lift the GitHub protection that blocks force pushes and deletion.
  - For now `main` is also the release branch: it moves forward from `jusprin-dev` when a version is released, and releases are built from it. This may change if a separate release branch is added later.
- `jusprin-v1` holds JusPrin 1, for fixes to that version only.
- `jusprin-v2-poc` holds the experiments described below.
- Take each OrcaSlicer release into `jusprin-dev` as `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` rule 10 describes.

## Releasing

`.github/workflows/jusprin_release.yml` builds a release into a draft on GitHub; its top comment says how to start it. It refuses the commit until it has all of these:

- The version, in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/Version.hpp`, above every released JusPrin version.
- The release notes, in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Packaging/release-notes/<version>.md`.
- The Sentry secrets: `JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN`, the project the app sends error reports and crashes to, and `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`, `SENTRY_URL`, `SENTRY_ORG` and `SENTRY_PROJECT`, which upload each build's debug files and the pages' source maps. A platform's build fails unless Sentry then holds debug information with file and line for the app's own code (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Packaging/sentry_debug_files.sh`) and a source map for each page as built (`sentry_page_maps.sh` beside it); the nightly build checks the same.
- The guide, `docs/guide/`, checked for that version. Run `scripts/check_guide.py --ask-ai` on a built copy of the commit, fix every page it reports, and commit the pages with their pictures, skills and `docs/guide/checked-version.txt`, as `docs/guide/README.md` describes under "Before a release". That file names the version the check last passed for, not the commit. Ticking "Release without the guide check" on the workflow's Run workflow form skips this, and the draft's title then says so. A release started by pushing a `jusprin-release/` branch has no form, so it always needs the file.

## Error handling

Someone pastes a key from their own AI service, and the service refuses it because of a setting in their account. Only they can change that setting. Later the app loses a chat because of a mistake in our code. Only we can fix that. Every failure is like one of these: there is someone who can do something about it, and error handling is the work of getting the failure to them, in a form they can use.

A failure that is the person's has to reach them in words they can understand, saying truthfully where the problem lies and what to do next. When the other side, meaning the service, printer or system that refused, has already said this in words written for a person, show those words and say who said them, because it knows the situation better than a sentence we prepared. Two causes that leave the person doing the same thing share one sentence, since a second sentence tells them nothing more. Nothing is wrong with the app itself, so it carries on.

A failure that is ours has to reach us with everything the code knew, because we will have to find the cause. The person can do nothing with that detail. They need to know only that the fault is not theirs, and to have a way to send it to us. We write no code to deal with such a failure. Its cause is something we did not understand when we wrote the code, so any handling would be a guess, and a guess carries on in a state nobody can vouch for and hides the failure. The work stops.

Sending a failure to the wrong one is the mistake this section exists to prevent, and it can be made in both directions. Tell the person the service could not be reached when our server failed, and they check their network while we never hear of it. Tell them something went wrong on our side when their own account is out of credits, and they wait for us while our reports fill with things we cannot fix, until the ones we can fix are hard to see.

So look at the failure itself, with what the other side actually said, and work out whose it is. Usually it says. What we have prepared does not change the answer: a failure that is the person's stays theirs when nobody wrote a sentence for it. When it truly cannot be told, it comes to us, because a report we cannot use costs us one look, while a failure of ours that only the person saw is lost.

Sometimes that someone is neither the person nor us. A service the person chose, such as the AI service their own key is for, is down, overloaded or failing on its own side: whoever runs it can fix it, and nobody here can. The person still needs the truth, that the trouble is at that service and not with them or with JusPrin, so they stop looking for something to fix. It is not reported, because a report is for someone who can act on it. Behind a JusPrin account the AI service is ours, because we chose it and can change it, so its failures come to us.

A failure we know people will meet is part of the feature, and the feature is not finished until the person who meets it is told what to do. Every failure is also written to the log, whoever it goes to. The log is where we look when a report or a question sends us looking. It tells nobody anything by itself.

### In practice

- Whose a failure is depends on its cause, such as "out of credits" or "no network", both of them the person's. A status code, an exception type, or the way the failure arrives (an HTTP status, an event inside a reply) is not a cause.
- A branch for "anything else" decides for every failure nobody listed. A failure the other side says is the person's goes to the person, and one that cannot be told comes to us. One sentence there for failures with different owners is a guess.
- A sentence we write for the person needs Kenneth's yes; quote his words in the commit message. Each has a test, and each time it is shown is counted. Showing the other side's own words needs no sentence of ours.
- A failure that is the person's, or that nobody here can fix, is handled with normal control flow, not exceptions, and is not reported.
- A failure that is ours gets one sentence, "Something went wrong on our side", and a way to report it. Do not sort such failures into kinds for the person, and do not bring Kenneth a question about the wording of one. On 2026-11-16 the code that kept five "try again" sentences apart was deleted for this reason.
- A failure that is ours stops the work and travels up unchanged. Do not catch it, give it a default value, retry it, or give it a sentence of its own.
- A failure that arrives as a value, such as a status code, stops nothing by itself. Once it is clear that it is ours, or that it cannot be told whose it is, turn it into a thrown error on the spot and keep the other side's status, request id and error text.
- One handler at the top of each entry point reports through `report_unexpected_error` (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Support/ErrorReport.hpp`) and tells the person. No other code reports. In the code, a failure that comes to us is called unexpected, and any other is called expected.
- The report carries the other side's status, request id and error text, and the request's own facts, such as the user, the chat, the turn and the model.
- When our own code is on both ends, a message that is refused or cannot be read is ours.
- One exception to "the work stops" and "no other code reports": a tool call that fails is shown as failed in the turn's activity line, its error goes to the AI model, and the turn goes on. When the failure is the app's own and not the model's mistake, it is also reported, with no dialog, and for this kind of failure only if the person has turned automatic reports on.
- Never record a failure as a success.

### Catching

- Catch a failure only when the code knows what it is and can recover from it, or at a boundary to translate it or add context, and then rethrow.
- Keep lower-level operations strict; the caller that owns the workflow enforces their preconditions.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering.

### Checks

- An agent reads the changed code against this section. Of each failure the code decides on, with what the other side really says, it asks: whose is it, and does it reach them in a form they can use?
- To audit a commit range, use the `error-handling` skill (`.claude/skills/error-handling/`). To check production for a period, use the `jusprin-production-check` skill in the tsd-enterprise repository.

## Build Commands

Build the Release configuration unless asked otherwise.

```bash
# macOS
cmake --build build/arm64 --config Release --target all --

# Linux
cmake --build build --config Release --target all --

# Windows
cmake --build . --config Release --target ALL_BUILD -- -m
```

Node/npm is required to build the Agent and Home pages, or configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply the bundles.

### Building on a shared machine

Several agent sessions build on the same Mac at once. Without a limit, ninja runs one compile job per core plus two, so every build you start can take the whole machine. In 2026-10 one session stacked four builds in one build directory: 56 clang processes on 12 cores. It kept restarting its build to change targets and never limited the job count.

- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. If the load is already above the core count, wait or build less.
- Limit jobs: `cmake --build … -- -j4`.
- Decide the full target list before starting. Never restart a running build to add or change targets: let it finish, then build the rest.
- Run one build per build directory. Two ninja processes in one directory compete and can leave its records inconsistent.
- Stopping a build means stopping ninja. `pkill -f "cmake --build …"` kills only the cmake wrapper, and ninja keeps compiling. Start long builds in their own process group (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV' cmake --build …`) and stop them with `kill -- -<pgid>`. Then confirm with `pgrep -fl ninja` before building again.
- When a build is slow, count your own compile processes before blaming the load on other sessions.
- Reuse an existing build where the task allows. Ask before configuring a fresh full-app build the task does not require.
- Before building against a dependency folder built earlier, such as the main checkout's `deps/build/arm64`, run `scripts/deps_current.sh <folder>`. It rebuilds the libraries whose `deps/` recipe changed since that folder was built.

## Testing

Catch2 framework. Tests in `tests/`; see [tests/AGENTS.md](tests/AGENTS.md) for where a new test belongs and the conventions to follow.

```bash
cd build && ctest -C Release --output-on-failure    # all tests
ctest --test-dir ./tests/libslic3r -C Release       # individual suite
ctest --test-dir ./tests/fff_print -C Release
```

Printer UI without hardware: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` (Bambu in-process fake); Moonraker and OctoPrint: `tests/printer_hosts/README.md` (Docker). Isolated `--datadir`; do not drive another JusPrin instance.

## Documentation

- Docs live in `docs/`; the high-level design of a subsystem goes in `docs/HLSD/<subsystem>.md`.
- Describe the design as it stands — what the subsystem does, why it exists, and the constraints that shape it. Not the route that got there: no phases, task lists, status markers, or "before/after this PR" framing.
- Planning and investigation output (brainstorms, superpowers design and plan docs) stays in `docs/superpowers/`, which is gitignored. Never commit it.
- Write a doc only when the design is not evident from the code, and when a change invalidates an existing one, update it in the same PR.

## Code Style

- C++17, selective C++20. PascalCase classes, snake_case functions/variables
- `#pragma once` for headers. Smart pointers and RAII preferred
- Include what you use: include the header for every symbol a file uses, and keep headers compilable on their own. Never rely on the precompiled header or a transitive include. The `clang-tidy` CI job enforces this on changed lines; run the same check locally with `scripts/run_clang_tidy.sh` (`scripts\run_clang_tidy.ps1` on Windows), which sets up everything it needs
- Parallelization via TBB — be mindful of shared state
- Wording: a file or object is "opened", "imported", "loaded" or "added", never "arrived". "Arrive" is fine for messages, responses, events and lists. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards the text the model reads.
- Wording the model reads calls the product "the app", never Orca or OrcaSlicer: the model speaks as the app, and a second name reads as a second program. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards this too. Log lines may name Orca. A throw may only if it never reaches the model: tool results forward save and open errors as they are, and the guard does not see those strings.
- Always use `SetSizerAndFit(sizer)` instead of `SetSizer(sizer)` on top level window. Unless `SetSizer` must be called before the full layout is built, call `sizer->SetSizeHints(window)` afterwards in this case.

## Key Entry Points

- App startup: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp`
- Slicing pipeline: `src/libslic3r/Print.cpp`
- All print/printer/material settings: `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`
- GUI: `src/slic3r/GUI/`
- Core algorithms: `src/libslic3r/` (GCode/, Fill/, Support/, Geometry/, Format/, Arachne/)
- Printer profiles: `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`

## JusPrin Production UI

- Start with `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md` for the canonical product definition, production architecture, verification method, Orca integration guidance, and design system.
- Before editing any file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`. Every line changed in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase, so those changes must be small, product-neutral, additive where possible, and accompanied by the rebase evidence that document requires.
- Experimental plans, probes, screenshots, logs, and temporary UI code remain on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Use `agent-docs/jusprin/poc-reference.md` for exact commit and path pointers; do not cherry-pick the POC wholesale.
- Curated brand and semantic UI assets live under `resources/jusprin/`.
- Before writing or changing any UI code, native or Agent page, follow "Writing UI code" in `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md`: every color, radius, font, and control size comes from the token file through `ShellTheme`, the shell recipes, or the CSS variables. A value with no token gets a token and a guard first, never a literal.
- Before designing a screen or writing any on-screen text, follow `agent-docs/jusprin/design-guidelines.md`: whole-screen boards with real strings, the wording rule, and a cold-reader check on screenshots before and after building.
- Temporary working docs (handoffs, findings, plans written for another agent) stay untracked: never commit them, and never add them to `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude`. Untracked files in `git status` are how Kenneth tracks work that isn't finished.

## Critical Constraints

- **Backward compatibility required** for .3mf project files and printer profiles
- **Cross-platform** — all changes must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux
- Profile/format changes need version migration handling
- Dependencies built separately in `deps/build/`, then linked to main app

## Pull requests

Before opening a pull request or posting on GitHub, read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), including its "If you are an AI agent" section.

## Code review focus areas

- Changes must not cause regressions in existing functionality, defaults, profiles, or project compatibility.
- Features gated by options must not affect existing behavior when those options are disabled.
- Changes should follow the existing code style and architecture. Architectural changes should be justified in code comments and the PR description.
- Add helper functions or utilities only when existing code cannot reasonably be reused. Avoid duplication.
- Changes to OrcaSlicer-owned files must be additive where possible. Rewriting an upstream function, or reimplementing upstream behavior beside it, needs explicit justification in the PR description.
- When an upstream line is deleted or relocated, say where it went and what a future rebase must carry into the new home.
- Keep code concise and clear. Manually simplify AI generated bloated codes before review.
- Include targeted tests or documented verification for behavior changes, especially in slicing logic, profiles, formats, and GUI defaults.
- For profile changes (`resources/profiles/<Vendor>/**`), check that `version` in the sibling `resources/profiles/<Vendor>.json` was bumped.
- For new or changed UI strings, check they follow [Writing translatable strings in the source](#writing-translatable-strings-in-the-source): no concatenated fragments, plural forms for counts, contexts for ambiguous words.
- For translation changes (`localization/i18n/**/*.po`), check that recurring terms match the [Localization glossary](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_glossary.md) for that language.

## Localization & translations

Catalogs live in `localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`; the template is `OrcaSlicer.pot`.
See the [Localization guide](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_guide.md) for the human-facing version of these principles.

### Writing translatable strings in the source

Translators see one msgid at a time and cannot change the code around it, so each message must be complete in a single msgid. Use the wrapper that fits instead of assembling text from pieces:

- **One msgid per sentence, with placeholders.** Never build a message by concatenating translated fragments (`_L("A") + name + _L(" is B")`) or by splicing a translated word such as `_L("left")` into another sentence: the translator can't reorder or inflect the parts. Write `format(_L("%1% is too close to others"), name)`.
- **A count needs a plural form.** Don't write `file(s)` or leave a verb unchanged after a number. Use `_L_PLURAL("%1% object", "%1% objects", n)`. libslic3r has no plural lookup, so word the message so it doesn't depend on a count, or build it in the GUI.
- **An ambiguous word needs a context.** When a short string means different things in different places (verb or noun, a mode name, a CAD term), give each sense its own context with `_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`/`L_CONTEXT`. Keep the most common sense without a context so its existing translations stay valid.
- **Mark every user-visible string** (`_L`/`_u8L`, or `L` where it is translated later) and list new source files in `localization/i18n/list.txt`: files that aren't listed are never extracted.
- Add a `// TRN` comment above a new string whose meaning or placeholders aren't obvious.
- Never choose behavior by comparing translated text; compare ids or flags.

See `.claude/skills/orca-translations/references/source-audit.md` for the full checklist.

### Terminology

- Use the [Localization glossary](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_glossary.md) as the source of truth for recurring terms, so the same English term is always rendered the same way within a language, and terms that must stay in English (brand/product names, acronyms, materials, file formats, G-code tokens, macros/variables/identifiers) are not translated.
- If a term's established translation changes, update both the affected `.po` files and the glossary (`developer_reference/glossary/<lang>.tsv` in the wiki, then regenerate) so they stay in sync.
- Translate the *meaning*, not the words. Check what the string actually controls before translating it — English reuses one word for different things. `Flow ratio` (multiplier), `Flow Rate` (throughput) and `Flow Dynamics` (pressure compensation) are three different terms; `extruder` may mean the toolhead, the feeder motor, or the nozzle depending on the string.
- Reuse one template per recurring message shape (`Failed to connect to …`, `Are you sure you want to …?`), even where the English wording varies.

### Editing rules

- Only edit `msgstr` — **never** change `msgid`, and never "fix" wrong English in the translation alone. Report the source string instead.
- Preserve exactly: placeholders (`%s`, `%d`, `%1%`, `%zu`, `%%`), every `\n` (count *and* position, including leading/trailing), leading/trailing spaces, HTML tags, `℃`, and the file's encoding and line endings.
- **Never reorder positional arguments** in a `c-format` string. If the msgid is `%d` then `%s`, that order must hold — swapping them breaks at runtime.
- `msgctxt` separates homonyms — always read it. `Back`/`Camera View` is the rear view of the 3D navigator, while `Back`/`Navigation` is the go-back button; `Top` exists in the *Alignment*, *Layers* and *Camera View* senses.
- When a string needs disambiguating, add context in the source (`_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`), don't work around it in the translation.
- A literal `%` inside a string xgettext flagged `possible-c-format` will fail `msgfmt`. Fix it with a `// xgettext:no-c-format, no-boost-format` comment above the string in the source — do not mangle the translation or use `%%` in text that is never passed through printf.
- Plural entries: read `nplurals` from the catalog's `Plural-Forms` header (it is **not** always 2 — ja/ko/zh/th/vi use 1, ru/cs/pl/lt use 3, uk uses 4). Each form must be genuinely inflected for its quantity; repeating one sentence across all forms is a bug in Slavic/Baltic languages, though it is correct for Turkish and Hungarian.
- An entry whose `msgstr` equals its `msgid` is untranslated even though it is not empty; a plural entry with any empty form is likewise incomplete.
- Mark machine-produced translations with an `# AI Translated` translator comment. Don't add it to a human translation you didn't actually rewrite.
- When you can't be sure of a machine translation's meaning or UI wording, also add `# Needs human review: <what to check>`. Never use `fuzzy` for this — fuzzy entries are hidden from users.
- Don't reflow or re-wrap unrelated entries — keep the diff limited to the strings you changed.

### Verifying

- `scripts/run_gettext.bat --full` (Windows) regenerates the template, merges every catalog and compiles the `.mo` files. It must exit 0.
- Or check a single catalog with `msgfmt --check-format --check-header -o <out>.mo localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`. Without `--check-header`, msgfmt skips the placeholder check in plural forms.
- Fuzzy entries are not shown to users. If you correct one, clear its `fuzzy` flag, otherwise the fix never ships.
